clues.title: Street sign: Street name ending - tee
text: In Estonia, the words for street and road are "tänav" and "tee," respectively. If you see street signs ending in "tee" or "tn" (with "tänav" often abbreviated as 'tn'), you know you're in Estonia.

clues.title: Bollard: Bollards
text: Estonian bollards have a **round, baton-like shape**.
They have a **rectangular** reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back. The reflectors can be white or orange.
**NOTE:** Latvian and Lithuanian bollards look different.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Short Dashes
text: Outer road lines sometimes consist of **short dashes**.
**NOTE:** Lithuania also sometimes has short dashes.
Be careful not to confuse this with Sweden which also uses short dashes.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Chevron: Chevrons
text: Estonia uses **red chevrons** with **white arrows**.
**NOTE:** Russia and Ukraine use the same chevrons.
However, Latvian and Lithuanian chevrons have the opposite colour scheme: they are white with red arrows.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: KM Markers
text: All Baltic countries use the same blue kilometre marker. However, they can be distinguished from each other by their angle relative to the road.
In Estonia, the marker will be **perpendicular** to the road. It has numbers on both sides of the marker.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Sign: Sign Border
text: Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
Estonian signs have a **thin red border**, with **no white outline** around it (the red border extends all the way to the edge of the sign).

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Guardrail: Guardrails
text: Estonia has normal A-type guardrails with **no reflectors**.
**NOTE:** The other two Baltic countries can have reflectors on their guardrails.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pedestrian sign: Pedestrian Signs
text: Estonian pedestrian signs have **3 stripes**. Best way to differentiate from other 3 striped crossing is that Estonia pedestrian signs have the **head attached** to the figure.
**NOTE:** Lithuanian signs also have 3 stripes, but the pedestrian looks less detailed.
Latvian pedestrian signs have 5 stripes.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Direction sign: Blue&White Wrappings

clues.title: Street sign: Street Names
text: The Estonian words for street and road are **tänav** and **tee**, respectively. These words are unique to Estonian. Tänav is often abbreviated as **‘tn’**.
Many streets, especially in urban areas, have a simple name that completely lacks the tänav and or tee suffix.

clues.title: Thin Roads

clues.title: Language: Estonian
text: Estonian is a Finnic language closely related to Finnish. It is **not** related to Latvian or Lithuanian. Within the Baltic languages, the following letters are unique to Estonian:
Vowels with umlauts (two dots): **Ä, Ö**, and **Ü**. Ä and Ö also exist in Finnish, but not Ü.
**Õ** with a tilde. This letter is one of the best ways to identify Estonian. Portuguese also uses it however, but mixing up Estonian and Portuguese is hard because they are otherwise very different.
The Estonian word for street is **tänav**, very commonly abbreviated as **tn**.
The Estonian word for road is **tee**. This is unlike Finnish which uses **tie**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
